title: SQL interview practice
summary: Practise the SQL patterns interviewers love — joins, aggregation, grouping, and window functions — and explain your query out loud.
objectives: Read a question, identify the tables, and plan the query before typing
Choose the right join (INNER vs LEFT) for the question asked
Aggregate with GROUP BY and filter groups using HAVING
Solve top-N-per-group problems with window functions
Know the logical order SQL actually runs clauses in
Explain your query out loud the way an interviewer expects

quiz.q: Which join keeps every row from the left table even when there is no match on the right?
quiz.why: LEFT JOIN returns all left-table rows; columns from the right table are NULL where no match exists.

quiz.q: WHERE filters individual rows. Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
quiz.why: HAVING runs after GROUP BY, so it can filter on aggregates like COUNT(*) > 5; WHERE cannot.

quiz.q: In what order does SQL logically evaluate these clauses: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY?
quiz.answer: FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then SELECT (SELECT runs near the end).
quiz.why: Because SELECT runs late, column aliases defined there are not visible to WHERE or GROUP BY in most engines.

quiz.q: You need the 2nd highest salary per department. Which tool fits best?
options: A window function like RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
quiz.why: Window functions rank rows within each partition without collapsing them, which is exactly what top-N-per-group needs.

quiz.q: Why can COUNT(column) return a smaller number than COUNT(*) on the same table?
quiz.answer: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(column) ignores rows where that column is NULL.
quiz.why: Knowing NULL handling shows the interviewer you think about data quality, not just syntax.

quiz.q: True or false — an INNER JOIN can return fewer rows than either input table.
quiz.why: True. Unmatched rows from both sides are dropped, so the result can be smaller than both inputs.

body_markdown:
## Why SQL still wins interviews

Almost every data and A I role touches data that lives in a relational database, so **SQL** comes up in interviews far more than people expect. The good news: the question patterns repeat. Master a handful of them and you can solve most live screens calmly.

This lesson is about *practice*, not memorising syntax. The skill interviewers grade is: can you read a vague question, picture the tables, and turn it into a correct query while talking through your reasoning?

## Start by reading the data, not writing code

Before you type, identify the **tables**, their **keys**, and which one is the "main" table the answer is about. Restate the question in plain English: *for each customer, count their orders*. That sentence already tells you the join and the GROUP BY.

```sql
-- For each customer, how many orders have they placed?
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
```

Notice the **LEFT JOIN**: a customer with zero orders still appears, with a count of 0. An INNER JOIN would silently hide them — a classic interview trap.

## Joins, GROUP BY, and HAVING

- **INNER JOIN** keeps only matching rows from both sides.
- **LEFT JOIN** keeps every left row, filling NULLs where the right has no match.
- **GROUP BY** collapses rows into groups so you can aggregate (COUNT, SUM, AVG).
- **HAVING** filters those groups *after* aggregation; **WHERE** filters rows *before*.

```sql
-- Customers who have spent more than 1000 in total
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 1000;
```

## The logical order of execution

SQL does not run top to bottom. The logical order is roughly: **FROM** -> **WHERE** -> **GROUP BY** -> **HAVING** -> **SELECT** -> **ORDER BY** -> **LIMIT**. Because SELECT runs late, an alias you create there usually cannot be used in WHERE. Saying this in an interview signals real understanding.

## Window functions for top-N-per-group

When a question says "per group" and "top N" or "second highest", reach for a **window function**. Unlike GROUP BY, it ranks rows *without* collapsing them.

```sql
-- Top earner per department
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM (
  SELECT name, department, salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) ranked
WHERE rnk = 1;
```

## Practice plan before your screen

Do a few easy and medium database problems on LeetCode or SQLZoo each day. **Speak your plan out loud** before typing, watch for NULLs, and always sanity-check row counts. Calm, narrated reasoning beats a silently typed perfect query.

slides.title: SQL interview practice
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Six, where we get you interview ready. In this lesson we focus on S Q L, which shows up in almost every data and A I interview. We'll practise the handful of patterns that come up again and again, and just as important, how to talk through your answer the way an interviewer wants to hear it.

slides.title: Why SQL in interviews?
bullets: Almost every data role queries a database.
The question patterns repeat.
They grade reasoning, not memorised syntax.
slides.narration: So why does S Q L matter so much? Almost every data and A I role touches data sitting in a relational database, so it comes up far more than people expect. The good news is that the patterns repeat. And what interviewers really grade is your reasoning: can you turn a vague question into a correct query while thinking out loud.

slides.title: Read the data first
bullets: Identify the tables and their keys.
Restate the question in plain English.
That sentence reveals the join and grouping.
slides.narration: Before you type a single character, slow down and read. Find the tables, find the keys that connect them, and decide which table the answer is really about. Then restate the question in plain English, like, for each customer count their orders. That one sentence already tells you the join and the group by you'll need.

slides.title: Counting per group
bullets: LEFT JOIN keeps customers with zero orders.
GROUP BY collapses rows into groups.
COUNT aggregates each group.
slides.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS n
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
slides.narration: Here's the classic count per customer. Notice we use a left join, not an inner join. That means a customer with zero orders still shows up, with a count of zero. An inner join would silently drop them, and that is a very common interview trap. Group by collapses the rows, and count does the tally.

slides.title: Joins you must know
bullets: INNER keeps only matching rows.
LEFT keeps every left row, NULLs on the right.
INNER can return fewer rows than both inputs.
slides.narration: There are two joins you absolutely must be fluent in. An inner join keeps only rows that match on both sides. A left join keeps every row from the left table, filling in nulls where the right side has no match. And remember, an inner join can return fewer rows than either input table, because unmatched rows simply disappear.

slides.title: WHERE vs HAVING
bullets: WHERE filters rows before grouping.
HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
HAVING can test COUNT or SUM.
slides.code:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 1000;
slides.narration: People mix these two up constantly. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens. HAVING filters the groups afterwards, so it can test an aggregate like sum of amount greater than one thousand. If your filter mentions count or sum, you almost certainly want HAVING, not WHERE.

slides.title: Logical order of execution
bullets: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING.
Then SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
SELECT aliases aren't visible to WHERE.
slides.narration: S Q L does not run top to bottom the way it's written. Logically it goes from, then where, then group by, then having, and only then select, order by, and limit. Because select runs near the end, an alias you create there usually can't be used back in your where clause. Saying this out loud in an interview signals real understanding.

slides.title: Window functions
bullets: Use them for top-N or rank per group.
PARTITION BY splits into groups.
Rows are ranked, not collapsed.
slides.code:
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM (
  SELECT *, RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
    ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) t
WHERE rnk = 1;
slides.narration: When a question says per group and top N, or second highest, reach for a window function. Partition by splits the data into groups, and rank assigns a position within each group. Unlike group by, it ranks the rows without collapsing them. We wrap it in a subquery and then filter to rank equals one to get the top earner in every department.

slides.title: Watch for NULLs
bullets: COUNT(*) counts all rows.
COUNT(col) skips NULLs in that column.
NULLs also vanish in inner joins.
slides.narration: Nulls quietly change answers, so mention them. Count star counts every row, but count of a column ignores rows where that column is null, so it can be smaller. Nulls also disappear in inner joins. Pointing out null handling shows the interviewer you think about data quality, not just syntax.

slides.title: Practice plan
bullets: Do easy and medium problems daily.
Speak your plan before typing.
Always sanity-check the row counts.
slides.narration: Here's your plan. Do a few easy and medium database problems each day on LeetCode or S Q L Zoo. Crucially, speak your plan out loud before you type, the way you will in the real interview. And after every query, sanity-check the row counts. Calm, narrated reasoning beats a silently typed perfect answer.

bullets: Read the tables before writing code.
INNER vs LEFT, GROUP BY vs HAVING.

Task: solve five database problems, talking aloud.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Always read the tables and restate the question before writing a line. Know the difference between inner and left joins, and between where and having. Use window functions when you need top N per group. And remember the logical order of execution. Your task before the next lesson: solve five database problems, and narrate your reasoning out loud each time. Great work, and I'll see you next lesson.
